source_text: Adhuc adiciam illam quoque partem in qua dum haereticus quasi oculo quodam gaudet proprio, ueritatis et luminis amisso, totam caecitatem sui agnoscat erroris. identidem enim et frequenter opponit quia dictum sit: sano tempore uobiscum sum, et non agnoscitis me? Philippe, qui uidit me, uidit et patrem. sed quod non intellegit, discat. culpatur Philippus, et iure quidem meritoque, quia dixerit: domine, ostende nobis patrem, et sufficit nobis. quando enim ex Christo aut audierat istud aut didicerat, quasi esset pater Christus, cum contra magis, quod filius esset, non quia pater, frequenter audisset, et saepe didicisset? quod enim dixit dominus, s me cognouistis, et patrem meum cognouistis, et a modo nostis illum, et uidistis illum, non sic dixerat ut se patrem uellet intellegi, sed quoniam qui penitus et plene et cum tota fide et tota religione accessit ad dei filium, omnibus modis per ipsum filium, in quem sic credit, ad patrem peruenturus sit, eundemque uisurus. nemo enim, inquit, potest uenire ad patrem nisi per me, et ideo ad patrem deum non tantum uenturus est, et cogniturus ipsum patrem, sed etiam sic tenere debet, atque ita animo ac mente praesumere, quasi iam nouerit patrem pariter et uiderit. Saepe enim scriptura diuina, quae nondum facta pro factis annuntiat, quia sic futura sunt, et quae omnibus modis fieri habent, non quasi futura sint, praedicat, sed quasi facta sint, narrat. denique cum nondum temporibus Isaiae prophetae Christus natus fuisset, quia puer, aiebat, natus est nobis; et cum nondum accessum esset ad Mariam, e accessit ad propheten, dicebat, e concepit, et peperit filium. et cum nondum sinum patris Christus exposuisset, referebat: e uocabitur nomen eius magni consili angelus. et cum nondum fuisset passus, guas? outs, pronuntiabat, ad iugulationem adductus est. et cum adhuc crux nusquam esset, aiebat: Tota die expandi manus meas ad populum non credentem., et cum nondum iniuriose potatus fuisset, s7fz, ait, mea potauerunt me aceto. et cum spoliatus adhuc non fuisset, dicebat, super uestem meam miserunt sortem: et dinumerauerunt ossa mea: effoderunt manus meas et pedes. prouidens enim scriptura diuina pro factis dicit, quae futura scit, et pro perfectis dicit, quae futura habet, quae sine dubitatione uentura sunt. et ideo dominus in praesenti loco dicebat: a modo nostis illum, et uidistis. dicebat enim uisum iri ab eo patrem, quisquis filium secutus fuisset; non quasi filius ipse esset pater uisus, sed quod praemium consecuturus esset, quisquis illum sequi et discipulus eius esse uoluisset, ut uidere patrem posset. nam et imago est dei patris, ut his etiam illud accedat, quoniam sicut pater operatur, ita operatur et filius, et imitator est filius omnium operum paternorum; ut perinde habeat unusquisque, quasi iam uiderit patrem, dum eum uidet qui inuisibilem patrem in omnibus operibus semper imitatur. Ceterum si ipse pater est Christus, quomodo confestim adicit et dicit: gud credit in me, opera quae ego facio et ipse Faciet, et maiora his faciet, quia ego ad patrem uado? et adhuc subnectit: si diligitis me, praecepta mea seruate: et ego rogabo patrem, et alium aduocatum dabit uobis. post quae etiam illud subnectit: s quis me diligit, sermonem meum custodiet: et pater meus diliget illum, et ad eum ueniemus, et mansionem apud illum Jaciemus. nec non etiam subdidit illud quoque: aduocatus autem ille spiritus sanctus, quem missurus est pater, ille uos docebit et commemorabit- omnia quaecumque dixero. praemittit adhuc istum locum, quo ostendat se esse filium, et merito subdidit, et dicit: s me diligeretis, gauderetis, quia eo ad patrem: quia pater maior me est. quid autem cum etiam ila subnectit: ego sum uitis uera, et pater meus agricola: omne sarmentum in me non afferens fructum tollit illud, et omne fructtSerum purgat, ut fructum ampliorem ferat? instat adhuc et adicit: sicut dilexit me pater, et ego dilexi uos; manete in mea caritate; si mandata mea seruaueritis, manebitis in mea caritale, sicut ego patris mandata seruaui, et maneo in eius caritate. adhuc ingerit, et dicit: dixi autem uos amicos, quia omnia quae audiui a patre meo, nota uobis feci. aggregat etiam hoc: sed haec omnia facient uobis propter nomen meum, quia ignorant eum qui me misit. Haec ergo numquam post illa euidenter illum non patrem sed filium esse testantia dominus subdidisset, si aut patrem se esse meminisset, aut patrem se uellet intellegi. nisi quoniam ut illud exprimeret, perinde unumquemque iam habere debere, dum imaginem dei patris per filium uidet, atque si uiderit patrem—quandoquidem unusquisque credens in filium exerceatur in imaginis contemplatione, ut assuefactus ad diuinitatem uidendam imagine proficere possit et crescere usque ad dei patris omnipotentis perfectam contemplationem,—et quoniam, qui hoc animo ac mentecombiberit et de omnibus sic futurum esse crediderit, patrem, quem uisurus sit, quasi iam quodammodo uiderit et hic iam sic habeat, quasi teneat, quod habiturum se pro certo sciat. Ceterum, si ipse pater fuisset, quid quasi futurum praemium repromittebat, quod iam praestiterat et dederat? nam quoniam dicit: beati mundo corde, quia ipsi deum uidebunt, polliceri deprehenditur contemplationem et aspectum patris. ergo nondum dederat: cur enim repromitteret, si iam dedisset? dederat enim, si pater esset; uidebatur enim, et contingebatur. quando autem, dum contingitur ipse Christus et uidetur, repromittit tamen et dicit, quoniam qui mundo fuerit corde, deum uidebit, hoc ipso probat patrem se non esse, qui tunc praesens cum uideretur repromittebat, quod patrem uisurus esset quisquis mundo corde fuisset. erat ergo repromittens haec non pater sed filius; quia qui filius erat, quod uideri habebat repromittebat: cuius repromissio superuacua fuisset, nisi filius fuisset. cur enim repromittebat mundis ut uiderent patrem, Si iam tunc qui praesentes erant, patrem Christum uidebant? sed quia filius erat, non pater, merito et filius, quia imago dei, tunc uidebatur, et pater, quia inuisibilis, mundis corde, ut uideretur, repromittitur et notatur. Haec igitur satis sit etiam aduersus istum haereticum dictasse, pauca de multis. campus enim, et quidem latus ac fusus, aperietur, plenius haereticum istum si agitare uoluerimus; quandoquidem duobus istis locis quibusdam effossis luminibus orbatus, totus sit in doctrinae suae caecitate superatus.
pass_a_gloss: I will also add that part in which, while the heretic, as it were, rejoices with his own eye, having lost the truth and light, may recognize his total blindness of error. For he frequently opposes the fact that it was said: I am with you in healthy times, and you do not recognize me? Philip, who saw me, also saw the Father. But what he does not understand, let him learn. Philip is blamed, and rightly and deservedly so, because he said: Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us. For when did he hear or learn from Christ that Christ was the Father, whereas, on the contrary, he heard and learned more frequently that He was the Son, not the Father? For what the Lord said, If you have known me, you have also known my Father, and from now on you know Him, and you have seen Him, He did not say this so that He might be understood as the Father, but because whoever approaches the Son of God with total faith and religion will, through the Son, come to the Father and see Him. For no one, He says, can come to the Father except through me, and therefore, one will not only come to the Father and know Him, but also must hold and presume in mind and spirit as if one already knows and sees the Father. For divine Scripture often announces what has not yet been done as if it were already done, because it will be so, and what will happen in all ways, not as if it were going to happen, but as if it had already happened. Finally, when Christ had not yet been born in the time of the prophet Isaiah, it was said: A child has been born to us, and before He had come to Mary, it was said to the prophet: He has come and conceived and borne a son. And when Christ had not yet laid His breast against the Father's breast, it was said: His name will be called the Angel of great counsel. And when He had not yet suffered, it was proclaimed: He was led to slaughter. And when the cross did not yet exist, it was said: I have stretched out my hands all day to a disobedient people. And when He had not yet been given vinegar to drink, it was said: They gave me vinegar to drink. And when He had not yet been stripped, it was said: They cast lots for my garment, and they numbered my bones, and they pierced my hands and feet. For divine Scripture speaks of what will be done as if it were already done, and of what will be perfected as if it were already perfect, because it knows what will happen without a doubt. And therefore, the Lord said in this place: From now on you know Him, and you have seen Him, for He said that the Father would be seen by whoever followed the Son; not that the Son Himself was the Father seen, but that whoever followed Him and wanted to be His disciple would receive the reward of seeing the Father. For the Son is the image of God the Father, so that it may be added that, just as the Father works, so also the Son works, and the Son is the imitator of all the Father's works, so that each person may have it as if they had already seen the Father, while seeing the One who always imitates the invisible Father in all His works. But if Christ Himself were the Father, how could He immediately add and say: He who believes in me will do the works that I do, and he will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father? And He also adds: If you love me, keep my commandments, and I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Advocate. And after this, He also adds: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him. And He also adds: The Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send, will teach you and remind you of all that I have said. He anticipates this place to show that He is the Son, and rightly adds and says: If you loved me, you would rejoice, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I. And what about when He also adds: I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer, and every branch that does not bear fruit in me will be taken away, and every fruitful branch will be purified, so that it may bear more fruit? He also adds: As the Father loved me, so I have loved you; remain in my love; if you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love, just as I have kept the Father's commandments and remain in His love. He also says: I have called you friends, because I have made known to you all that I heard from my Father. He also adds: But they will do all this to you on account of my name, because they do not know the One who sent me. Therefore, the Lord would not have added these things, which clearly testify that He is not the Father but the Son, if He had remembered that He was the Father or wanted to be understood as the Father. Unless it was to express that each person ought to have it as if they had already seen the Father, while seeing the image of God the Father through the Son, and as if they had seen the Father, since each believer in the Son is exercised in the contemplation of the image, so that, having become accustomed to seeing the divinity in the image, they may progress and grow until they reach the perfect contemplation of God the Father Almighty. But if He Himself were the Father, what reward would He promise as if it were still to come, when He had already given and bestowed it? For since He says: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God, He is found to promise the contemplation and vision of the Father. Therefore, He had not yet given it; why would He promise it if He had already given it? He would have given it if He were the Father; for He would have been seen and touched. But when Christ, while being touched and seen, still promises and says that whoever is pure in heart will see God, He proves by this very fact that He is not the Father, who, being present and visible, promises what one will see when they are pure in heart. Therefore, it was not the Father but the Son who was making these promises, because, being the Son, He was promising what was to be seen; and His promise would have been unnecessary if He were not the Son. Why would He promise the pure in heart that they would see the Father, if those who were already present were seeing the Father, Christ? But because He was the Son, not the Father, and rightly so, since He is the image of God, He was seen at that time, and the Father, being invisible, is promised to be seen by the pure in heart. These things, then, are sufficient, even against this heretic, to have said a few things out of many. For the field, which is wide and spacious, will be opened if we want to discuss this heretic further; since, having been blinded by the removal of two passages, he is completely overcome by the blindness of his doctrine.

Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me.

pass_b_english: I will add one more section, the one in which the heretic, as it were, rejoices with his own eye even though he has lost the truth and the light, so that he may recognize the total blindness of his error. He repeatedly and frequently objects that it was said, "I am with you in healthy times, and you do not recognize me? Philip, who saw me, also saw the Father" (John 14:9). But what he fails to understand, let him learn. Philip is blamed, and rightly and deservedly so, because he said, "Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us." When, after all, did he ever hear or learn from Christ that Christ was the Father? On the contrary, he heard and learned far more often that He was the Son, not the Father. For what the Lord said, "If you have known me, you have also known my Father, and from now on you know Him and have seen Him" (John 14:11), He did not say in order to be understood as the Father Himself, but because whoever approaches the Son of God with total faith and total religion will, through that very Son, come to the Father and see Him. No one, He says, can come to the Father except through Me; therefore, one will not only come to the Father and know Him, but must also hold and presume in mind and spirit as if one already knows and sees the Father. Divine Scripture often announces things not yet done as if they were already done, because they will certainly be so, and it narrates things that must happen in every way not as future events but as accomplished facts. For example, when Christ had not yet been born in Isaiah's time, it was said, "A child has been born to us"; before He had come to Mary, it was said to the prophet, "He has come, and conceived, and borne a son"; before Christ had revealed the Father's bosom, it was reported, "His name will be called the Angel of Great Counsel"; before He had suffered, it was proclaimed, "He was led to slaughter"; before the cross existed, it was said, "I have stretched out My hands all day to a disobedient people"; before He had been given vinegar to drink, it was said, "They gave Me vinegar to drink"; before He had been stripped, it was said, "They cast lots for My garment, and they numbered My bones, and they pierced My hands and feet." Divine Scripture speaks of future things as already done, and of future perfections as already perfect, because it knows without doubt that they will come. Therefore the Lord said in this place, "From now on you know Him and have seen Him," for He said the Father would be seen by whoever followed the Son — not that the Son Himself was the Father seen, but that whoever followed Him and chose to be His disciple would receive the reward of seeing the Father. The Son is the image of God the Father, so that it may be added that just as the Father works, so also the Son works, and the Son is the imitator of all the Father's works; thus each person may have it as if he had already seen the Father, while seeing the One who always imitates the invisible Father in all His works. But if Christ Himself were the Father, how could He immediately add and say, "He who believes in Me will do the works I do, and will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father"? And He adds further: "If you love Me, keep My commandments, and I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Advocate." After this He also adds: "If anyone loves Me, he will keep My word, and My Father will love him, and We will come to him and make Our dwelling with him." And He also adds: "The Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send, will teach you and remind you of all that I have said." He anticipates this passage to show that He is the Son, and rightly adds and says: "If you loved Me, you would rejoice, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I." What about when He also adds: "I am the true vine, and My Father is the farmer; every branch in Me that does not bear fruit He takes away, and every fruitful branch He purifies, so that it may bear more fruit"? He insists and adds: "As the Father loved Me, so I have loved you; remain in My love; if you keep My commandments, you will remain in My love, just as I have kept the Father's commandments and remain in His love." He also says: "I have called you friends, because I have made known to you all that I heard from My Father." He also adds: "But they will do all this to you on account of My name, because they do not know the One who sent Me." The Lord would never have added these things, which clearly testify that He is not the Father but the Son, if He had remembered that He was the Father or had wanted to be understood as the Father — unless it was to express that each person ought to possess it as if he had already seen the Father, while seeing the image of God the Father through the Son, and as if he had seen the Father; since every believer in the Son is exercised in the contemplation of the image, so that, having become accustomed to seeing the divinity in the image, he may progress and grow until he reaches the perfect contemplation of God the Father Almighty — and since whoever drinks this in with mind and spirit and believes that all things will be so, holds the Father he will see as if he had already seen Him and already possesses Him here, because he knows for certain he will possess Him. But if He Himself were the Father, what future reward would He promise, when He had already given and bestowed it? For since He says, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God," He is found to promise the contemplation and vision of the Father. Therefore He had not yet given it; why would He promise it if He had already given it? He would have given it if He were the Father, for He would have been seen and touched. But when Christ, while being touched and seen, still promises and says that whoever is pure in heart will see God, this very fact proves He is not the Father, who, being present and visible, promised what the pure in heart would see — the Father. Therefore it was not the Father but the Son who made these promises, because, being the Son, He promised what was to be seen; and His promise would have been superfluous unless He were the Son. Why would He promise the pure in heart that they would see the Father, if those then present were already seeing the Father in Christ? But because He was the Son, not the Father, and rightly so, since He is the image of God, He was seen at that time, and the Father, being invisible, is promised and made known to the pure in heart as the One who will be seen. These things, then, are sufficient to have said against this heretic, a few out of many. For a field, wide and spacious, will be opened if we wish to pursue this heretic further; since, blinded by the removal of two passages, he is completely overcome by the blindness of his doctrine.
